Version history
1.0 broke making the cursor not blinking in Vim mode; a previously working CSS snippet to fix it stopped working.
Obsidian is my favorite app, only missing feature is better PDF support like Logseq, which lets you embed and annotate PDFs with markdown, area highlights, math notation.
Obsidian is less opinionated on the file format and folders, making it more future-proof than Logseq, though Logseq's sync is too asynchronous requiring manual reindexing across devices.
As an outliner, Logseq is too opinionated about usage; Obsidian is less strict, allowing mixing Zettelkasten, daily notes, and folder structures freely.
Bases is essentially a 90% replacement for the Dataview plugin, much faster and more responsive, though not yet as comprehensive.
Dataview's dataviewjs mode lets you write custom imperative JavaScript to dynamically render content in notes, a capability Bases (queries-to-tables) doesn't replicate.
There's no decent RAG functionality among Obsidian AI plugins, but the Text-Generator plugin with links/backlinks pulled into inference context has been the most productive LLM interface for years.
The Git plugin is great for single-device backup but not great for device sync or collaboration; a real-time collaboration plugin using CRDTs was built to add Google-docs style collab to Obsidian.
The Obsidian Android app does not save files to storage until the note unloads, which can break things if you sync/pull mid-edit, sometimes causing missing last lines.
Confirmed via Obsidian's own docs: there is no sandboxing at all for community plugins - every plugin has full access to your computer's filesystem and can make network requests.
A company wrote a sandboxed alternative app because community plugins are too risky running with full system access when working on sensitive data.
Obsidian being closed-source makes it harder to verify their security model compared to note-taking systems where all plugin code is visible and scannable by the user.

One thing bugs me: I cannot create a desktop shortcut to open a specific Obsidian vault directly, since a vault is a folder not a recognizable file; also F2 rename shortcut doesn't work, adding friction.
Obsidian Canvas uses a new JSON-based file format, open-sourced under MIT license; canvas files remain local and still link to your own future-proof Markdown files.
This looks like Obsidian's first move away from markdown - the .canvas JSON files are readable but not as readable as markdown; hope this isn't a trend toward proprietary formats.
While Canvas is interesting, adding such a large feature raised concern - worry that Obsidian could end up like Evernote, which did too much and became bloated.
Used Obsidian for organizing and running tabletop RPG sessions with folders of monsters, encounters, and world notes; also good enough to replace Sublime + directory for daily dev note-taking.
I dislike the aesthetics and wouldn't use Obsidian because of Electron; spoiled by native note apps like Bear and Noteplan on macOS with nicer UX/UI, especially on mobile.
Moved from Google Docs to Obsidian for de-Googling; notes stored only locally and via storage sync, files are just text so notes can outlive the app itself.
Migrated from Roam to Obsidian and it's really awesome - ownership of files, constant updates with new features and bug fixes, and a really nice community.
